title: IV Medication Drip Rate Calculation
problem: ICU nurses continuously titrate high-risk IV drips (vasopressors, sedatives, insulin, heparin) based on patient response. Manual calculation of mcg/kg/min to mL/hr under time pressure leads to dosing errors. A single miscalculation with a vasopressor can cause fatal hypotension or hypertensive crisis.
who: Staff ICU nurses and new grad ICU nurses titrating multiple drips simultaneously

skill_spec.name: ICU Drip Rate Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Converts medication dose orders (mcg/kg/min, units/hr, mg/hr) to IV pump rate in mL/hr and vice versa

outputs.name: time_to_empty
outputs.label: Estimated time until bag runs out

skill_spec.formula_hint: rate_mL_hr = (ordered_dose * weight_kg * 60) / (concentration_mg / volume_ml * 1000) for mcg/kg/min; adjust formula per dose_unit type

example_queries: Calculate drip rate for norepinephrine 0.15 mcg/kg/min, patient 82kg, concentration 4mg in 250mL
I have propofol running at 25 mL/hr, concentration 10mg/mL, patient weighs 70kg - what's the mcg/kg/min?
Heparin 25,000 units in 250mL, ordered at 1,200 units/hr - what pump rate?

title: Fluid Balance and I&O Calculation
problem: ICU nurses track all intake (IV fluids, medications, blood products, tube feeds) and output (urine, drainage, blood loss) hourly. End-of-shift totals require adding dozens of entries across 12 hours. Errors in fluid balance calculation can mask fluid overload or dehydration, leading to pulmonary edema or renal failure.
who: All ICU nurses managing critically ill patients with complex fluid needs

skill_spec.name: ICU Fluid Balance Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates total intake, output, net fluid balance, and cumulative balance over shift with itemized breakdown
skill_spec.formula_hint: net_balance = total_intake - total_output; urine_ml_kg_hr = urine_output / (weight_kg * hours); flag if UO < 0.5 mL/kg/hr

example_queries: Calculate 12-hour fluid balance: 2000mL LR, 500mL albumin, 150mL med volume, urine 850mL, JP drain 200mL, patient 75kg
My patient got 3 liters total intake and put out 1100mL urine in 12 hours, weight 68kg - what's the balance and urine output per kg?
Is urine output of 25mL/hr adequate for an 80kg patient?

title: Hemodynamic Parameter Calculation
problem: Nurses monitoring Swan-Ganz catheters and arterial lines must calculate MAP, SVR, cardiac index, oxygen delivery, and other derived hemodynamic values to guide vasopressor and fluid management. These calculations involve multiple variables and formulas that are easy to miscalculate at 3 AM during a code.
who: ICU nurses managing hemodynamically unstable patients with invasive monitoring

skill_spec.name: Hemodynamic Parameter Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates MAP, SVR, SVRI, CI, DO2, VO2, and other derived hemodynamic values from monitored inputs
skill_spec.formula_hint: MAP = (SBP + 2*DBP)/3; SVR = (MAP-CVP)/CO * 80; CI = CO/BSA; BSA = 0.007184 * height^0.725 * weight^0.425; DO2 = CO * (Hgb * 1.34 * SaO2) * 10

example_queries: Calculate MAP, SVR and cardiac index: BP 88/52, HR 112, CVP 14, CO 3.8, height 170cm, weight 80kg
Patient has CO of 5.2, Hgb 9.2, SaO2 94% - what's the oxygen delivery?
SVR for MAP 62, CVP 8, cardiac output 4.5?

title: ABG Interpretation and Acid-Base Analysis
problem: ICU nurses receive ABG results multiple times per shift and must quickly interpret pH, PaCO2, PaO2, HCO3, base excess, and lactate to identify acid-base disorders and oxygenation status. Mixed disorders (e.g., combined metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis) are common in ICU patients and difficult to interpret. Delayed recognition can delay ventilator adjustments or treatment of sepsis.
who: All ICU nurses, especially those managing ventilated patients

skill_spec.name: ABG Interpreter and Acid-Base Analyzer
skill_spec.one_liner: Interprets arterial blood gas results, identifies primary and mixed acid-base disorders, calculates A-a gradient and P/F ratio
skill_spec.formula_hint: AG = Na - (Cl + HCO3); corrected AG = AG + 2.5*(4.0 - albumin); A-a gradient = (FiO2*(713) - PaCO2/0.8) - PaO2; P/F = PaO2/FiO2; Winter's formula: expected PaCO2 = 1.5*HCO3 + 8 +/- 2

example_queries: Interpret ABG: pH 7.28, PaCO2 32, PaO2 68, HCO3 15, lactate 4.2, Na 140, Cl 104, albumin 2.8, FiO2 60%
Patient on vent FiO2 50%, PaO2 88 - what's the P/F ratio and does this qualify as ARDS?
ABG shows pH 7.52, PaCO2 28, HCO3 22 - is this pure respiratory alkalosis or mixed?

title: Ventilator Settings and Weaning Assessment
problem: ICU nurses must understand and monitor ventilator settings (mode, tidal volume, PEEP, FiO2, respiratory rate) and assess patient readiness for weaning. Incorrect tidal volume calculations based on ideal body weight can cause ventilator-induced lung injury. Missed weaning windows prolong ventilation and increase VAP risk.
who: ICU nurses managing mechanically ventilated patients

skill_spec.name: Ventilator Calculator and Weaning Readiness Tool
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates ideal body weight, lung-protective tidal volumes, static/dynamic compliance, RSBI, and assesses weaning readiness
skill_spec.formula_hint: IBW male = 50 + 2.3*(height_in - 60); IBW female = 45.5 + 2.3*(height_in - 60); Target TV = IBW * 6-8 mL/kg; Static compliance = TV/(Pplat - PEEP); RSBI = spontaneous_RR / spontaneous_TV; weaning likely if RSBI < 105

example_queries: Calculate ideal body weight and target tidal volume for a 5'9 male on the vent
Patient on CPAP/PS has spontaneous RR 28 and tidal volume 0.22L - what's the RSBI? Ready to extubate?
Static compliance with TV 450, plateau 28, PEEP 10?

title: High-Risk Medication Double-Check
problem: ICU nurses administer high-alert medications (vasopressors, insulin, heparin, paralytics, potassium) that have narrow therapeutic windows. Independent double-checks are required by policy but often rushed or skipped during emergencies. Medication errors in ICU settings have higher mortality rates than on general floors.
who: All ICU nurses, especially during night shifts with limited pharmacist availability

skill_spec.name: ICU High-Alert Medication Verification Checklist
skill_spec.one_liner: Step-by-step independent double-check process for high-alert ICU medications with dose range verification
steps: Step 1: Verify correct patient (two identifiers - name and DOB/MRN)
Step 2: Confirm medication matches order (drug name, route, dose, frequency)
Step 3: Check medication concentration against standard ICU concentrations
Step 4: Verify dose is within safe range for patient weight
Step 5: Confirm IV pump rate calculation matches ordered dose
Step 6: Check compatibility if running with other IV lines
Step 7: Verify monitoring parameters are in place (e.g., glucose checks for insulin, PTT for heparin)
Step 8: Confirm allergies reviewed
Step 9: Assess current vitals against medication parameters (hold parameters)
Step 10: Document second nurse verification with time and initials
warnings: WARNING: Insulin and heparin are the #1 and #2 causes of ICU medication errors
WARNING: Neuromuscular blockers must NEVER be given without sedation verification
WARNING: Concentrated potassium (>20 mEq/hr) requires cardiac monitoring
WARNING: Vasopressor concentration changes require complete rate recalculation

example_queries: Walk me through the double-check process for starting a vasopressin drip
What's the verification checklist for hanging a new heparin bag?
I'm about to give IV push potassium 20 mEq - what do I need to verify?

title: ICU Shift Handoff Report
problem: ICU shift handoffs (every 12 hours) require communicating massive amounts of critical patient data - ventilator settings, drip rates, labs, procedures, family wishes, code status, and pending orders. Incomplete handoffs are a leading cause of ICU adverse events. Nurses spend 30-45 minutes preparing and giving report.
who: All ICU nurses during shift change

skill_spec.name: ICU SBAR Shift Handoff Report Generator
skill_spec.one_liner: Generates a structured ICU handoff report using SBAR format with all critical systems and pending items

variables.name: renal_fluid
variables.label: Renal/Fluid: I&O, labs, CRRT if applicable

variables.name: gi_nutrition
variables.label: GI/Nutrition: diet, tube feeds, bowel function

variables.name: skin_wounds
variables.label: Skin/Wounds: Braden score, pressure injuries, drains

skill_spec.structure_hint: SBAR format -> Situation (1 line summary) -> Background (diagnosis, hx, hospital course) -> Assessment (head-to-toe by system) -> Recommendation (plan, pending, watch-for items)

example_queries: Help me organize my handoff report for a septic shock patient on 3 vasopressors and CRRT
Generate a shift report template: 68yo M, CABG post-op day 1, on vent, neo drip, chest tubes
I need to give report on my ARDS patient - help me structure it by body system

title: Sepsis Screening and Bundle Compliance
problem: Sepsis is the #1 killer in ICUs. CMS requires hospitals to follow SEP-1 sepsis bundle with strict time-based metrics (lactate within 6 hours, blood cultures before antibiotics, 30mL/kg crystalloid within 3 hours). Nurses are responsible for recognizing sepsis early and ensuring all bundle elements are completed on time. Missing a single element affects hospital quality scores and reimbursement.
who: All ICU nurses, especially those receiving new admissions and transfers

skill_spec.name: ICU Sepsis Bundle Compliance Tracker
skill_spec.one_liner: Tracks all CMS SEP-1 bundle elements with time stamps, calculates fluid resuscitation volumes, and flags overdue items
steps: Step 1: Screen for SIRS criteria (temp >38.3 or <36, HR >90, RR >20, WBC >12k or <4k)
Step 2: Identify suspected infection source
Step 3: HOUR 1 BUNDLE - obtain lactate level
Step 4: HOUR 1 BUNDLE - obtain blood cultures (2 sets) BEFORE antibiotics
Step 5: HOUR 1 BUNDLE - administer broad-spectrum antibiotics
Step 6: HOUR 3 BUNDLE - if lactate >= 4 or hypotension: begin 30mL/kg crystalloid bolus
Step 7: Calculate 30mL/kg fluid volume for patient weight
Step 8: If hypotension persists after fluids: initiate vasopressors (target MAP >= 65)
Step 9: HOUR 6 - repeat lactate if initial was >= 2
Step 10: Document all bundle elements with exact times in EHR
Step 11: Reassess volume status and tissue perfusion
Step 12: Notify physician of any missed bundle element immediately
warnings: WARNING: Blood cultures MUST be drawn before first antibiotic dose
WARNING: Each hour delay in antibiotics increases mortality ~7.6%
WARNING: 30mL/kg fluid calculation uses actual body weight - document if physician modifies for heart failure
WARNING: CMS audits exact timestamps - late documentation = non-compliance
regulatory_refs: CMS SEP-1 Severe Sepsis/Septic Shock Early Management Bundle

example_queries: My patient is 92kg with suspected UTI sepsis, lactate 4.8 - walk me through the sepsis bundle and fluid volume
When does the sepsis clock start? What needs to happen in the first hour?
Patient had blood cultures drawn at 14:00 and antibiotics at 14:45 - are we compliant with SEP-1?

title: CCRN Certification and License Renewal Tracking
problem: ICU nurses juggle multiple certifications with different renewal cycles: CCRN every 3 years (requires 100 CERPs or retesting), ACLS/BLS every 2 years, PALS every 2 years, state RN license annually or biennially. Missing a renewal can result in inability to work, loss of pay differential, or legal liability for practicing with expired credentials.
who: All certified ICU nurses, especially travel nurses with multi-state licenses

skill_spec.name: ICU Nurse Certification and License Renewal Guide
skill_spec.one_liner: Quick reference for renewal requirements, deadlines, CE hours, and costs for all ICU nursing certifications and licenses
skill_spec.data_domain: Nursing certification and licensure renewal requirements for critical care nurses

data_hints.source_law: State Nurse Practice Acts, AACN Certification Corporation

key_data_points.ccrn_renewal: Every 3 years, 100 CERPs or retest, ~$175 renewal fee
key_data_points.rn_license: Varies by state - annual or biennial, 20-30 CE hours typical
key_data_points.compact_license: NLC allows practice in 41 member states with one license

example_queries: When does CCRN expire and how many CERPs do I need to renew?
What are the CE requirements for RN license renewal in California vs Texas?
I'm a travel nurse - do I need separate licenses for each state or can I use a compact license?

title: ICU Nurse Staffing Ratio Compliance
problem: Multiple states now mandate nurse-to-patient ratios in ICUs (California 1:2, Oregon tightening to 1:4 by June 2026 for general and specific ICU ratios). Federal legislation is pending. Charge nurses must track ratios in real-time, document violations, and understand reporting requirements. Violations carry fines up to $30,000 per incident in California.
who: Charge nurses, nurse managers, and staff nurses in states with ratio mandates

skill_spec.name: ICU Staffing Ratio Compliance Reference
skill_spec.one_liner: State-by-state ICU nurse staffing ratio requirements, penalties, reporting obligations, and federal pending legislation
skill_spec.data_domain: State and federal nurse staffing ratio laws for ICU settings

data_hints.source_law: State Nurse Practice Acts, Nurse Staffing Standards for Hospital Patient Safety and Quality Care Act (2025)

key_data_points.oregon_icu: Tightening to 1:4 by June 2026, $200 per missed break
key_data_points.reporting: Most states require written staffing plans filed annually

example_queries: What's the required nurse-to-patient ratio for ICU in California?
What are the penalties if our unit is running 1:3 in California ICU?
What are Oregon's new staffing requirements taking effect in 2026?

title: Rapid Response and Code Blue Documentation
problem: During a code blue or rapid response, one nurse is designated as the recorder. They must document exact times of interventions, medications given (with doses), rhythm changes, vital signs, and team roles - all while chaos unfolds in real-time. Incomplete code documentation creates legal liability and hinders post-code quality review.
who: ICU nurses participating in or leading code blue events

skill_spec.name: Code Blue Documentation Generator
skill_spec.one_liner: Generates a structured code blue/rapid response documentation record with ACLS algorithm prompts and timestamp tracking

variables.name: event_type
variables.label: Event type (Code Blue / Rapid Response / MET)

skill_spec.structure_hint: Header (patient, event type, time) -> Initial assessment (rhythm, vitals) -> Chronological intervention log (time-stamped) -> Medication log -> Airway management -> Outcome -> Post-event orders -> Team members -> Family communication

example_queries: Help me document a code blue - patient found in VF at 02:15, 3 rounds of CPR, 2 shocks, epi x3, ROSC at 02:28
Generate a rapid response record for a patient with new-onset SVT, rate 180, who converted with adenosine
What should be included in code documentation for legal protection?

title: Early Deterioration Warning Signs Assessment
problem: Missing subtle signs of clinical deterioration is one of the top fears of ICU nurses. Recognizing early sepsis, impending respiratory failure, neurological decline, or hemodynamic instability before a full crisis requires integrating multiple data points. New ICU nurses especially struggle with pattern recognition that experienced nurses develop over years.
who: New graduate ICU nurses and nurses in their first 1-3 years of ICU practice

skill_spec.name: ICU Patient Deterioration Advisor
skill_spec.one_liner: Analyzes current vital signs, labs, and clinical findings to identify early warning patterns of deterioration and recommend escalation actions
skill_spec.expertise_area: Early recognition of clinical deterioration patterns in critically ill patients

example_queries: My patient's MAP has been trending down from 72 to 65 over 4 hours, urine output dropped to 20mL/hr, lactate went from 1.8 to 3.2 - should I be worried?
Patient is increasingly agitated, RR went from 18 to 28, SpO2 dropped from 96 to 92 on 4L NC - what could be happening?
Post-op CABG patient has new-onset AFib with RVR rate 142, BP holding at 100/60 - what's my priority assessment and when do I escalate?

title: ICU Sedation and Pain Assessment Scoring
problem: ICU nurses must continuously assess sedation depth (RASS scale), pain (CPOT or BPS for intubated patients), and delirium (CAM-ICU) to titrate sedatives and analgesics. Over-sedation prolongs ventilation and increases delirium risk. Under-sedation causes self-extubation and line removal. Balancing these scores with daily sedation vacations is complex.
who: ICU nurses managing sedated and mechanically ventilated patients

skill_spec.name: ICU Sedation, Pain, and Delirium Assessment Guide
skill_spec.one_liner: Quick reference for RASS, CPOT, BPS, and CAM-ICU scoring with target ranges, sedation vacation protocols, and titration guidance
skill_spec.data_domain: ICU sedation assessment scales, pain scoring for non-verbal patients, and delirium screening

data_hints.source_law: PADIS Guidelines 2018 (Pain, Agitation/Sedation, Delirium, Immobility, Sleep), SCCM Clinical Practice Guidelines

key_data_points.sedation_vacation: Daily spontaneous awakening trial unless contraindicated

example_queries: How do I score RASS? My patient opens eyes to voice but doesn't sustain eye contact
Patient is intubated and grimacing, pulling at tubes - how do I score CPOT?
Walk me through CAM-ICU assessment - patient seems confused and inattentive after sedation vacation

title: Moral Distress and Burnout Self-Assessment
problem: 25-33% of critical care nurses experience severe burnout, with 86% having at least one symptom. Moral distress from futile care situations, repeated patient deaths, and understaffing compounds over time. Nurses often don't recognize burnout until they're already in crisis. No structured self-assessment tools are readily available at the bedside.
who: All ICU nurses, especially those with 1-5 years of ICU experience

skill_spec.name: ICU Nurse Burnout and Moral Distress Advisor
skill_spec.one_liner: Provides confidential burnout self-assessment, identifies moral distress triggers, and recommends evidence-based coping strategies and resources
skill_spec.expertise_area: Critical care nurse mental health, burnout prevention, moral distress management, and resilience building

example_queries: I've been dreading going to work for the past month and I can't stop thinking about a patient who died on my shift - is this burnout?
We've had 5 deaths in my unit this week and I feel nothing anymore - is that normal?
What resources are available for ICU nurses dealing with moral distress from prolonged futile care?
